Scenario

The Manager’s complaint list needs a column showing how many days a complaint has been open — days_open — without storing it on the entity (it changes every day, so persisting it would immediately go stale). This is a textbook afterQ use case: compute it once, on the way out, from data already in the result set.
Implementing afterQ
Wiring days_open into the UI

Add days_open as a transient property (Session 5, Part D) on d_complaints so the Page Builder can bind a column to it, then add that column to s_complaints (Session 2, Part B.9.2). Because the value arrives already computed on the result row, no additional binding logic is needed on the client.

Developer Level 2 — Advanced Track Enhancing the Customer Complaints Application This track does not build a new application. Every session goes back into the SAME Customer Complaints app built in Developer Level 1, and layers a new advanced capability onto it — the same end-to-end build approach used in the Level 1 guide. Prerequisite: Developer Level 1 completion is mandatory. Proposed dates are placeholders (one session per working day, starting Mon 07 Sep 2026) — confirm actual start date and cadence.

Developer Level 1 was built as an end-to-end project: one real application — the Customer Complaints Application — built up session by session. This Level 2 guide follows the same approach: no new application is created. Every session below re-opens the entities, pages, entity files, and controllers already built in Level 1 and extends them with an advanced capability, so trainees see how real applications evolve rather than practicing features in isolation. Topics are drawn from the Training Topics sheet, filtered to entries tagged “Developer Level 2,” and mapped onto concrete enhancements of the existing app. Tool names use the current naming glossary, with legacy names noted where relevant.

Sessions must be taken in order — each session's steps assume the previous session's enhancement is already in place, exactly as in the Level 1 guide. Configure Network Modes so offline-relevant properties sync correctly to field devices. Apply Sort Order and an Entity Index to d_complaints for performance and predictable ordering. Extend the existing Entity Rules with a new auto-escalation rule. Extend the existing Query Rules with role-based field masking. Build a BOL Transaction that commits two entities atomically. What This Session Builds On Developer Level 1 (Sessions 1–5) built d_complaints with its properties, one Entity Rule (onCreateComplaint) and one Query Rule (beforeQ) on q_complaints. This session does not start a new entity — it goes back into the same d_complaints and q_complaints files and adds the advanced BOL capabilities on top.

A field IT Team member on a tablet needs complaint status and priority visible even with no signal, while internal notes stay server-side only. Meanwhile complaints are quietly sailing past SLA with no auto-flag, and a support rep spots that anyone on the IT Team can see a customer's full contact details in the list — details they never needed for their job.

Not every property should sync to a field device the same way. Configure Network Mode per property on d_complaints. # Action Detail 1 Open properties Procify Data Studio → d_complaints → Properties tab. 2 Restrict remark Set Network Mode = Online Only on remark — internal notes should not be cached on IT Team field devices. 3 Always sync core fields Set Network Mode = Always on complaint_id, s_status, priority so they remain visible even when the device is offline. 4 Save & update schema Save, then Update Schema, and confirm no errors.
documents.s: Part A — Network Modes — Offline-Ready Properties

documents.t: The complaints list currently has no defined default order and no index for the fields it is filtered on most. # Action Detail 1 Set Sort Order On priority: custom order CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW. On created_on: DESCENDING as the secondary sort. 2 Create Entity Index Entity Index tab → Add → ID: idx_complaint_status_priority — fields: s_status, priority. 3 Update Schema Update Schema and verify the index is listed under the entity's Test → Data Browser diagnostics.
documents.s: Part B — Sort Order & Entity Index

documents.t: Reopen the same d_complaints.ts file from Level 1 Session 5 and add a second rule alongside onCreateComplaint. # Action Detail 1 Register the rule Rule tab → Add → Event Type: On Update | Channel: Always on Server | Clazz: this | Invocation Method: checkEscalation. 2 Implement checkEscalation If s_status is OPEN or INPROCESS and (today − created_on) > 3 days, set is_escalated = true. 3 Test Backdate a test record's created_on in Data Browser to 4 days ago, save, and confirm is_escalated flips to true.
documents.s: Part C — Entity Rules — Auto-Escalation on Update

documents.t: Extend q_complaints.ts — the same file where beforeQ was written in Level 1 Session 4 — with an afterQ rule. # Action Detail 1 Add afterQ Event Type: After Query. In the handler, if the requesting role is IT_TEAM, replace customer contact fields in each result row with ‘•••’. 2 Test as IT Team Log in as it_<prid> — confirm customer contact fields are masked in the list. 3 Test as Manager Log in as mgr_<prid> — confirm the same fields show full data.
documents.s: Part D — Query Rules — Role-Based Field Masking

documents.t: Combine a status update and a new voice record into one atomic operation. # Action Detail 1 Create the transaction Data Studio → new BOL Transaction Tx_CloseWithFeedback, covering d_complaints (update s_status = CLOSED) and d_complaint_voices (create feedback record). 2 Wire the button Add a ‘Close with Feedback’ action on s_detail_header that commits both TransNodes through this transaction. 3 Test atomicity Force the voice record to fail validation (e.g. leave it blank) and confirm the status change also rolls back — not just the voice record. Session 1 Checkpoint ✔ Network Modes verified in an offline emulation for at least 3 properties. ✔ s_complaints defaults to priority order; idx_complaint_status_priority exists and is used. ✔ checkEscalation rule fires correctly on a backdated test record. ✔ afterQ masks customer fields for IT_TEAM but not for Manager. ✔ Tx_CloseWithFeedback commits both entities together or rolls back together. Enhancement delivered: Extends the existing d_complaints / q_complaints files from Level 1 (not a new entity) with offline sync control, performance indexing, automatic SLA escalation, field-level data masking by role, and an atomic close-with-feedback commit.
documents.s: Part E — BOL Transaction — Close Complaint with Feedback

documents.t: Build a reusable Embedded Section and use it on two different pages. Add Advanced kloControls (rating, file uploader) to the detail screen. Configure TransNode onArrive and navigateId behaviour. Debug the Session 1 server-side rule using Server-Side Debugging. Enable Auto Update Data so the Manager's list refreshes without manual action. What This Session Builds On p_complaints was built manually in Level 1 Session 2 and styled in Session 6; p_complaint_dashboard was built in Session 5. Both existing pages are extended here — no new page is created from scratch.

A Manager opens a complaint and has to hunt across screens to see whether this customer has complained before. A rep marks a complaint resolved but there's no way to capture how satisfied the customer actually was, or attach a photo of a damaged product without emailing it separately.

Build one timeline section and reuse it in two places. # Action Detail 1 Create the section New section s_complaint_timeline (screenType: timeline) bound to a TransNode combining voices and status-change history. 2 Embed in detail In pa_comp_details, add a new section, mark it Embedded, and point its source to s_complaint_timeline. 3 Reuse on dashboard Add the same embedded section to p_complaint_dashboard as a ‘Recent Activity’ panel — confirming true cross-page reuse.
documents.s: Part A — Embedded Section — Complaint Timeline

documents.t: Add two controls that were not covered in Level 1's basic control set. # Action Detail 1 Add kloRating On s_detail_header, add a kloRating control bound to a new transient property t_satisfaction_score, visible only when s_status = CLOSED. 2 Add kloFileUploader On the attachments section, add kloFileUploader bound to the d_complaints_attachment relation built in Level 1. 3 Full Preview Confirm the rating control only appears on closed complaints and the uploader stores a file record correctly.

Make the detail screen smarter about what loads automatically and where links resolve to. # Action Detail 1 Configure onArrive On the detail TransNode, set onArrive to auto-load the 5 most recent related voices — no extra click required. 2 Configure navigateId On the ticket_id link control, set navigateId so it always resolves to pa_complaint_details, whether clicked from p_complaints or the dashboard's embedded timeline. 3 Test both entry points Click a complaint from the main list, then from the dashboard timeline — confirm both land on the same detail area correctly populated.

Debug the rule written in Session 1 and make the Manager's grid self-refreshing. # Action Detail 1 Attach debugger Set a breakpoint inside checkEscalation in VS Code and attach to the running Private Node. 2 Step through Trigger a save on a test complaint and step through the rule execution line by line. 3 Enable auto refresh On s_complaints, set Auto Update Data = true with a 30-second interval. 4 Verify Create a complaint as Employee in one browser tab; confirm it appears in the Manager's grid within 30 seconds without a manual refresh. Session 2 Checkpoint ✔ s_complaint_timeline renders correctly on both p_complaints and p_complaint_dashboard. ✔ kloRating and kloFileUploader function as specified. ✔ onArrive auto-loads voices; navigateId resolves correctly from both entry points. ✔ Breakpoint debugging confirmed inside checkEscalation. ✔ Manager's grid auto-refreshes within 30 seconds of a new complaint being created. Enhancement delivered: Adds a reusable complaint-history timeline, a satisfaction rating and attachment capture on resolution, smarter auto-loading/navigation, and a self-refreshing Manager grid — all on the existing pages built in Level 1.
documents.s: Part D — Server-Side Debugging & Auto Update Data

documents.t: Enforce CRUD restrictions server-side using design-time Permissions. Restrict IT Team visibility to their own team's complaints using Row Wise Auth. Scope customer data by region using Data Access Rules. Audit a user's effective access using User Access Summary. Grant, use, and revoke a temporary elevated Role Permission, and confirm it in Permission Logs. What This Session Builds On Level 1 Session 7 hid or disabled buttons per role using Vienable — a UI-level control only. This session enforces the same rules at the platform/security level so they hold even if a user calls the API directly.

An IT Team member who left last month still has delete rights if they call the API directly, even though the button is hidden in the UI. A regional manager can see every customer's complaints nationwide instead of just their region, and after an override was granted during an incident, nobody can say who approved it or when it was revoked.

Configure real CRUD restrictions, not just hidden buttons. # Action Detail 1 Configure Employee Employee role: Create + Read only. 2 Configure Manager Manager role: Create + Read + Update + Delete. 3 Configure IT Team IT Team role: Read + Update only. 4 Test server-side block Log in as emp_<prid> and confirm Delete is blocked even if attempted outside the hidden button (e.g. via a direct API call).

Restrict IT Team to only the complaints assigned to their own team. # Action Detail 1 Configure the rule Row Wise Auth on d_complaints: IT_TEAM role only receives rows where responsible_team = current user's team. 2 Test Log in as it_<prid> — confirm only assigned complaints appear, even via direct navigation to a different complaint's URL.

Scope customer master data regionally and verify it. # Action Detail 1 Create the rule New Data Access Rule scoping d_customers by region. 2 Assign to Manager Assign the rule to mgr_<prid> for their region. 3 Verify with User Access Summary Open User Access Summary for mgr_<prid> and confirm the rule and effective permissions are listed correctly.
documents.s: Part C — Data Access Rules & User Access Summary

documents.t: Simulate an incident requiring temporary elevated access, then audit it. # Action Detail 1 Grant temporary access Create a runtime Role Permission override allowing IT_TEAM_LEAD to Delete during an incident. 2 Use and revoke Apply, test the elevated Delete, then revoke the override. 3 Audit in Permission Logs Confirm both the grant and the revoke appear in Permission Logs with timestamp and actor. Session 3 Checkpoint ✔ CRUD restrictions enforced server-side for all 3 roles. ✔ IT Team row-level filtering confirmed, including via direct URL access. ✔ Data Access Rule created, assigned, and confirmed via User Access Summary. ✔ Temporary Role Permission granted, used, revoked, and fully audited in Permission Logs. Enhancement delivered: Replaces Level 1's UI-only button hiding (Vienable) with rules enforced at the platform/security level, restricts IT Team visibility to assigned complaints, scopes customer data by region, and closes the audit gap on temporary access.
documents.s: Part D — Role Permissions (Runtime) & Permission Logs

documents.t: Enable offline access to assigned complaints for field IT Team users via Local Archive. Reduce first-login sync payload using Initial Downloads. Push closed complaints to an external SAP system via Middleware. Bulk-import customer master data using KloSectionXlsx. What This Session Builds On The application has only worked online through Sessions 1–3. This session makes it usable by IT Team members working onsite without connectivity, and adds a bulk-data path for customer onboarding.

An IT Team technician visiting a customer site with no signal can't pull up the complaint they're there to resolve. Every login re-downloads the full complaint history instead of just what's assigned, closed complaints aren't reaching the SAP billing system automatically, and onboarding 20 new customers means entering each one by hand.

Keep a working slice of data on the device for offline use. # Action Detail 1 Configure archive scope Local Archive on d_complaints and d_complaint_voices for the IT_TEAM role — retain the last 30 days of assigned complaints on-device. 2 Test offline On a device/emulator, disconnect network and confirm assigned complaints and their voice history are still viewable.

Reduce what gets pulled on first login. # Action Detail 1 Configure the download set Only OPEN/INPROCESS complaints assigned to the logging-in IT Team user are included in the first sync — not full history. 2 Verify Time a fresh login before and after the change and confirm a smaller payload.

Integrate with an external billing system. # Action Detail 1 Configure the channel New Middleware channel that pushes CLOSED complaints to an external SAP endpoint for billing reconciliation. 2 Test Close a test complaint and confirm the outbound payload appears in the middleware queue.

Add Excel-based bulk operations to the customer master entity. # Action Detail 1 Add to d_customers Attach KloSectionXlsx to the customer section, enabling bulk Excel upload/download. 2 Bulk import Prepare a sample sheet of 20 customers and import via the section. 3 Verify Confirm all 20 records land correctly in Data Browser. Session 4 Checkpoint ✔ IT Team can view assigned complaints and voice history fully offline. ✔ Initial download payload measurably reduced and verified. ✔ One closed complaint confirmed pushed to the SAP middleware queue. ✔ 20 customers successfully bulk-imported via KloSectionXlsx. Enhancement delivered: Makes the app usable in the field without connectivity, shrinks the first-login sync payload, automates the SAP billing hand-off on closure, and adds bulk customer onboarding.
documents.s: Part D — KloSectionXlsx — Bulk Customer Import

documents.t: Route escalated complaints through a Manager approval Workflow. Add a nightly Scheduled Task as a server-side safety net for SLA breaches. Notify the right people by Email, SMS, and In-App at the right moments. Deep-link notification emails directly into the relevant complaint. Configure an app-wide Banner for planned maintenance. What This Session Builds On Session 1 added a server-side is_escalated flag. This session adds the human workflow and communication layer that reacts to it.

A complaint sits open for a week past SLA with no one following up, because there's no approval step and no nightly check catching it. A customer is never told their complaint was resolved unless someone remembers to call, and a support email can't deep-link straight to the complaint it's about.

Give escalation a human decision point. # Action Detail 1 Build the workflow When is_escalated becomes true, route an approval task to the Manager to confirm reassignment of responsible_team. 2 Test Trigger escalation on a test complaint and confirm the Manager receives the task in Pending Approvals.

Add a server-side safety net independent of individual saves. # Action Detail 1 Create the task Scheduled Task that runs nightly, re-checking all OPEN/INPROCESS complaints against the 3-day SLA rule from Session 1. 2 Run manually and verify Trigger once via Running Tasks and confirm overdue complaints are correctly flagged.
documents.s: Part B — Scheduler — Nightly SLA Sweep

documents.t: Close the communication loop for assignment and resolution. # Action Detail 1 Assignment email Email notification to responsible_team the moment a complaint is assigned. 2 Resolution in-app alert In-App notification to the originating Employee when status changes to CLOSED. 3 Verify delivery Trigger both scenarios and confirm delivery in Notification History.

Make notifications actionable and announce planned downtime. # Action Detail 1 Configure deeplink The assignment email's ‘View Complaint’ link opens directly to the correct complaint detail screen. 2 Configure Banner App-wide banner announcing a planned maintenance window, visible to all roles for 24 hours. Session 5 Checkpoint ✔ Escalation approval task correctly routed to and actionable by the Manager. ✔ Nightly scheduler flags overdue complaints on a manual run. ✔ Assignment email and resolution in-app alert both confirmed delivered in Notification History. ✔ Deeplink opens the exact correct complaint; banner visible to all 3 roles. Enhancement delivered: Adds a human approval step on escalation, a nightly check independent of individual saves, closes the communication loop on assignment/resolution, and makes notifications actionable.

Replace static dashboard tiles with a live kloChart. Build an advanced TAT trend chart over a rolling 30-day window. Build a Pivot Modeller report for cross-team, cross-type analysis. What This Session Builds On Level 1 Session 5 built p_complaint_dashboard with static status-count tiles fed by status_count_query. This session replaces and extends those same tiles with real charts.

A Manager glances at the dashboard and sees numbers that were already stale this morning, with no way to see the SLA trend over the last month or drill into which team is falling behind — only static totals.

Turn the existing tile counts into a live chart. # Action Detail 1 Add the chart Add a kloChart bar chart to p_complaint_dashboard bound to the existing status_count_query TransNode. 2 Cross-check and replace Verify the chart's counts match the old static tiles, then remove the tiles.

Add a second, more advanced chart tracking service-level performance. # Action Detail 1 Build the query New query aggregating actual_tat vs standard_tat by week for the last 30 days. 2 Configure the chart Advanced line chart with two series (actual vs standard) and custom axis formatting.
documents.s: Part B — Advanced Chart — TAT Trend

documents.t: Give Managers a drillable cross-tab report. # Action Detail 1 Build the pivot Rows = complaint_type, Columns = responsible_team, Values = count of complaints, Filter = current month. 2 Publish & verify Publish to the EAM Portal and confirm a Manager can drill into a specific cell to see the underlying records. Session 6 Checkpoint ✔ Static dashboard tiles fully replaced by a live kloChart with matching counts. ✔ TAT trend chart renders 30 days of actual-vs-standard data. ✔ Pivot report published to EAM Portal and drill-down verified. Enhancement delivered: Replaces static dashboard tiles with live, trend-aware reporting and adds a drillable cross-tab view for Managers.

Diagnose a simulated scheduler failure end-to-end using platform monitoring tools. Confirm notification delivery and resolve a stuck offline sync record. Confirm the SAP middleware payload was processed via Legacy Queue Monitoring. Trace a native control rendering issue on a built APK. Independently verify dashboard numbers using Query Console. What This Session Builds On The app is feature-complete after Sessions 1–6 (automation, offline sync, integrations, reporting). This session is entirely about operating and troubleshooting what was built, not adding new features.

The nightly SLA sweep silently failed last night and nobody noticed until complaints started piling up unflagged. A customer insists they never got a resolution notification, and there's no way to check; finance says a closed complaint never showed up in SAP and nobody can tell whether it's stuck or lost.

Break the Session 5 scheduler on purpose, then find and fix it. # Action Detail 1 Simulate a failure Introduce a bad condition into the nightly SLA-sweep task and trigger it. 2 Observe the failure Confirm the failure appears in Scheduler Monitoring and Task History. 3 Trace the root cause Find the underlying error in Google Logs. 4 Fix and re-run Correct the task and confirm success via Running Tasks.

Confirm the Session 4 and 5 integrations are actually working end-to-end. # Action Detail 1 Verify notifications Check Notification History for the assignment/resolution messages from Session 5 — confirm delivered status. 2 Diagnose a stuck sync Simulate a stuck offline record on Server Queue / Mobile Sync Queue for an IT Team device from Session 4, and resolve it. 3 Check the SAP channel Review Legacy Queue Monitoring to confirm the Session 4 closed-complaint payload to SAP was processed.

Trace a native rendering issue and cross-verify reporting data. # Action Detail 1 Build and test the APK Build a debug APK including the kloRating control from Session 2. 2 Debug if needed If the control fails to render natively, use APK/IPA debugging tools to trace the issue. 3 Cross-verify dashboard data Use Query Console to independently confirm the raw row counts behind the Session 6 dashboard charts. Session 7 Checkpoint ✔ Simulated scheduler failure diagnosed via Scheduler Monitoring + Google Logs and resolved. ✔ Notification delivery confirmed; one stuck sync record identified and resolved. ✔ SAP payload confirmed processed in Legacy Queue Monitoring. ✔ APK rendering issue for kloRating traced (fixed or root-caused). ✔ Dashboard chart numbers cross-verified against raw data via Query Console. Enhancement delivered: Shifts the training from building features to operating and troubleshooting everything Sessions 1–6 put in place.

This final session prepares it for a real client rollout — a branded, inherited child flavor, migrated to QA.

The business is onboarding a new client, Acme, who needs their own complaint categories and branded login screen without touching the shared base app every other client depends on. Training Procedure Welcome to the Procify Developer Training. This section explains the overall structure of the course, how sessions are designed, and what is expected of you as a trainee. Read this before starting Session 1.

The training spans 8 sessions. Each session introduces a new layer of the platform — starting with setup and ending with publishing a fully working application. Sessions must be taken in order; each one builds directly on the previous. Session Topic Session 1 Platform Setup & Account Management Session 2 BOL — Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages Session 3 Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) Session 4 Value Helps & Queries Session 5 BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation Session 6 Bindings, Navigation & Styling Session 7 Controllers & Client-Side Behaviour Session 8 Menu Configuration & App Management, Versioning & Publishing

This training does not teach concepts in isolation. You will build one real application — a Customer complaint system — across all 89 sessions. Every concept is introduced exactly when you need it to make the next part of that application work. Why this matters for you You will always know WHY you are doing each step, not just HOW. By Session 8 you will have a working application demonstrating every major platform capability. The application grows session by session — if you miss a step it will affect later sessions. When you encounter a similar situation on a real project, you will have a concrete reference point from training.

Attend each session with the previous session's assignment completed and verified. Follow steps in this guide during hands-on time — do not skip ahead. Ask questions during the Review & Q&A phase, not during the trainer demonstration. The Application You Will Build This training guide uses a REAL application: the Customer complaints Application. You are not building a demo — you are building a production-ready application for delivery personnel. Every concept taught in every session is applied directly to build this application. By Session 9 you will have a fully working, published Delivery Agent Application.

By the end of this session, we will be able to: Understand the platform architecture. Create an application in the Workspace Hub. Define application roles and understand system vs. application roles. Create user accounts and assign them to an application with the correct role. Use Team Groups (User collections) to bundle multiple users and assign them to an application in a single, bulk step. Understands the role of data studio and page builder in application creation. ⚠ Why this session comes first The App you create today is built across ALL 9 sessions — treat it carefully. The Roles you define today are referenced in Session 5 (Validations) and Session 9 (Publishing access). The Users you create today are the test personas you will use to verify every screen built in Sessions 2–8.

Before touching any tool, you need a clear picture of the application you are building. Read this section carefully — every configuration decision in Sessions 1– traces back to this Business Requirement Document.
documents.s: Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application

documents.t: The Customer Complaints Application is a solution designed to manage customer complaints end-to-end across three personas: • Log and track customer complaints with full lifecycle management. • Route complaints from Employee → Manager → Responsible Team. • Manage complaint line items, voice records, and file attachments. • Monitor escalations, SLA (TAT), and resolution timelines. • Provide dashboards per role so every user sees what they need.

This application defines exactly three application roles, each mapped to a Procify role-rollup level for viewable and UI-Auth controls: Role ID Business Name Procify Role Rollup Employee Complaint Creator Owner (s_role_rollup = 10) Manager Complaint Assignor Supervisor (s_role_rollup = 20) Responsible Team Issue Resolver Reviewer (s_role_rollup = 30) 📘 Role Precedence Rule Precedence is a number. Lower = higher priority. Employee: precedence 3, Manager: precedence 2, ResponsibleTeam: precedence 1. This means if a user has multiple roles, the lower-precedence number overrides. Your developer account should be assigned Manager (precedence 2) for full access during testing.

The status lifecycle has 6 states. Each transition is triggered by a specific role: OPEN INPROCESS ON HOLD RESOLVED CLOSED REOPEN ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ Triggered by Employee Triggered by Manager / Responsible Team Triggered by Responsible Team Triggered by Responsible Team / Manager Triggered by Manager / Employee Triggered by Employee / Manager Status Badge Colour / Meaning OPEN Blue — complaint logged by Employee, awaiting Manager assignment INPROCESS Orange — Manager assigned responsible team; team working on it ON HOLD Purple — Responsible Team placed on hold pending information RESOLVED Green — Responsible Team marked as resolved CLOSED Grey — Manager confirmed resolution and closed the ticket REOPEN Red — Employee or Manager reopened a resolved/closed complaint 📘 Status Transition Rules OPEN → INPROCESS: only Manager can trigger (by assigning responsible_team).INPROCESS → ON HOLD / RESOLVED: only ResponsibleTeam can trigger.RESOLVED → CLOSED: only Manager can trigger.CLOSED → REOPEN: Employee or Manager can reopen; Reference: Workspace Hub 7.0 - User Guide Workspace Hub is an Admin Tool that focuses on managing applications and the application users. It is a versatile application that serves diverse purposes from user management to application management. Apart from that, this tool can also be used for modifying the already existing users and apps.

Workspace Hub menu will be visible for Users who are assigned as TESTER or DEVELOPER or SUPERADMIN for cockpit flavor. Step 1: Go to the menu options and select Workspace Hub. Step 2: The Workspace Hub contains the following Pages.

A User is a platform-level account — a person who can log in to one or more applications. Users exist independently of applications. You create the person first, then assign them to applications with roles separately. The same user can have different roles in different applications.

Create one test user to represent the end-user persona (emp01) throughout all sessions. 1 Navigate to Users In the Workspace Hub, click Users in the left navigation. The user list screen loads. 2 Click Create New User Click the create button in the toolbar. 3 Fill in User Details Complete all required fields as shown in the table below. Field What to enter Title Choose the title from dropdown (Mandatory) First Name Fill the first name (Mandatory) Last Name Fill the last name (Optional) Email A real or placeholder email address (Mandatory) Mobile Number used for OTP login if configured (Mandatory) Designation Fill the designation (Mandatory) User ID (Login ID) test_<your_prid> e.g. test_pr0045 BPID Choose bpid from dropdown (Mandatory) Authcode Choose authcode from dropdown (Mandatory) 4 Save the User Click Save. The user is created. Note the User ID — you will reference it when assigning this user to the application. You will complete that assignment in Part D of this session. If a user tries to log in before assignment, they will see error mentioning no applications assigned Refer Create User part from workspace hub manual for more information.

An application is a self-contained unit that holds all the metadata you build — entities, queries, pages, menus, and more. It is the primary organising structure of everything you will do in Sessions 2–8. Users are assigned to applications (with roles), not to individual Pages or features.

Roles control what a user can do inside the application. Procify has two categories: Role Type What it controls System Roles (built-in) MANAGER,DEVELOPER and TESTER— control access to dev tools (data studio,page builder, Workspace Hub, Private Node). Pre-built into the platform. Application Roles (custom) Roles you define inside your app. Control what users see and can do at runtime within your app's Pages and data. For this training, define single application role inside your app: Role Name Precedence Role Name DeliveryAgent 1 DeliveryAgent Role Precedence — Key Rule Precedence is a number. Lower number = higher priority. If a user has multiple roles, the one with the lowest precedence number takes effect at runtime. Delivery Admin(1) always overrides Delivery Agent(2) for a user assigned both roles. Your developer account will be Delivery Admin. The test user will be SRM_User. This lets you test both personas.

1 Open Your Application In the Apps list, click on srm_<prid> to open its detail screen. 2 Go to Roles & Users Click on the Roles & Users tab inside the application detail. 3 Create the DeliveryAgent Role In Application Roles, click Add. Assigning one test user at a time (as done in Part D) works fine for training, but it does not scale. Real projects onboard users in batches — a new hire cohort, an entire department, or a partner organisation that all needs the same app access on day one. Team Groups (labelled User collections inside the Workspace Hub screen) solve exactly this: they let you bundle a set of users once and assign the whole bundle to an application in a single step, instead of repeating the Part D steps per user. Team Groups are of two kinds: Individual Team Group — created automatically for every user the moment their account is created. Hidden by default (use the Show Individual checkbox to reveal them). Its only job is to let a newly created app be auto-assigned back to the user who created it. Group Team Group — created manually by an admin, and the one you will use for real onboarding work. It holds any number of users and can be linked to one or more App Collections (App Groups) so that every user in the group inherits access to every app in the collection Why Team Groups Matter in Practice Without Team Groups, assigning 25 new employees to 3 apps means 75 manual assignment actions (Part D, repeated). With a Team Group, it becomes: 1 group with 25 members, linked once to an App Collection with 3 apps. Team Groups are filtered by the logged-in user’s Auth Codes and scoped to the current landscape — you will only see groups you are authorised to manage.

The Customer Complaints BRD defines a ResponsibleTeam persona made up of several support agents, not just one test user. Rather than repeating Part D for each agent individually, model the onboarding the way a real project would:

Action Detail / Code Create the Team Group Navigate to Workspace Hub → User Collections (Team Groups). Click Add. Name it grp_response_team_<prid>. Add members Open the group, click Add under members, and select 3–4 existing users (or the test users created earlier in this session) to represent the support agents. Link to an App Collection Under the group’s App Groups tab, add the Customer Complaints App Collection so every member inherits the ResponsibleTeam role assignment. Verify in bulk Log in as any one member. Confirm the app is visible, exactly as verified individually in Part D — but this time achieved through the group, not a per-user step.

For onboarding sets larger than a handful of users, Team Groups also support bulk Excel upload/download, so a spreadsheet of usernames can populate group membership without clicking through the UI one row at a time. This is the same mechanism used for App Collections and is the recommended approach once a group exceeds roughly 10–15 members. 🛠 Hands-On — Try It Yourself Export your grp_response_team_<prid> group to Excel. Add two more (fictional) usernames as new rows. Re-upload the file and confirm the new rows appear as pending/invalid members (since those users don’t yet exist) — this is expected and demonstrates the validation Procify performs on upload.

Every application starts the same way: someone hands a developer a requirements document and says 'build this.' The Customer complaints Application Business Requirement Document (BRD) you read in Session 1 defines exactly what data needs to be stored — 3 data objects, their fields, and their relationships. The first job as a developer is to turn those definitions into a working database schema. Before opening any tool, it is worth understanding what that process looks like — and how much of it Procify eliminates. The rest of this part walks through the traditional process step by step, then shows exactly which steps the data studio replaces.
documents.s: Part E —  understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: 📘 Schema — The Blueprint of Your Application's Data A schema is the complete definition of the data your application stores: what tables exist, what columns each table has, what type of data each column holds, and how tables relate to each other. The schema is the foundation of every application. Without it, there is no database. Without a database, there is no data. Without data, there is no application. Building the schema is always the first development task after reading a BRD. Everything else — APIs, Pages, logic — is built on top of it. In our BRD, the schema is already defined in Section 4 (Entity Relationship Overview). The 4 entities, their properties, and their relationships are all there. Our job today is to implement that schema.

🏗 How developers build a schema without a low-code platform Step 1 — Write SQL scripts: A backend developer writes CREATE TABLE statements for each entity. For the Delivery table alone, that is 12 columns — each with its SQL data type, constraints, default values, and indexes. Step 2 — Write an ORM model: For every SQL table, the developer writes a model class in the backend language (Node.js/TypeScript, Python, Java). This class mirrors the database table and handles object-relational mapping. Step 3 — Write REST API endpoints: For each entity, the developer writes GET, POST, PUT, DELETE API handlers. Each handler validates input, maps it to the model, executes the database query, and returns the response. Step 4 — Write validation logic: For each property that has rules (mandatory, unique, min/max), the developer writes validation code — either in the model or in the API handler. Step 5 — Handle database migrations: Every time the schema changes (new property, renamed column), the developer writes a migration script to alter the existing tables without losing data. Step 6 — Test the API: The developer uses Postman or writes unit tests to verify each endpoint returns the correct data in the correct format. Repeat for all 4 entities. 🔴 The pain of the traditional approach Multiple files across multiple layers — SQL files, model files, API controller files, test files. A change to one field requires edits in 4–6 places. Context switching: a single developer must switch between SQL, backend language, API design, and test writing — each requiring a different mental mode. Time cost: 3–4 days of developer time before a single screen can be shown to a stakeholder. Repetition: most of this work is identical boilerplate — every entity needs the same pattern of SQL + ORM + CRUD APIs. Nothing creative, just repetitive.
documents.s: The Traditional Way of Building a Schema

documents.t: ✅ How Procifyreplaces the traditional schema-building process In Klobase, all 6 traditional steps are replaced by a single tool: the data studio. You define the entity (name, type) → add properties (name, data type, key attributes) → click Update Schema. Done. The platform automatically generates: the database table (SQL step 1), the data access layer (ORM step 2), the REST API endpoints (step 3), basic validation from key attributes (step 4), and handles schema updates automatically (step 5). There are no separate files to keep in sync. The data studio is the single source of truth. Everything downstream — API, data validation, mobile sync — is derived from it automatically. Time with Klobase: the same 4 entities, all properties, schema live in the database — approximately 2 hours in this session. The developer's time is freed for the parts that actually require thinking: business logic, UI design, user experience. This is not an approximation. Let us make it concrete: Traditional Task data studio Replacement Write CREATE TABLE SQL for Delivery entity Create entity in data studio — choose type, add properties, click Save Write ORM model class (12 fields × 4 entities) Already done — properties ARE the model Write 16+ REST API endpoints Already done — fireQuery apis are available to fetch data Write validation for mandatory fields Check the Mandatory key attribute icon on the property and validation will be handled by platform. Write database migration script Click Update Schema again — the platform handles ALTER TABLE automatically Test APIs with Postman Use the built-in Test function in the data studio toolbar

🔴 Traditional screen development requires five separate layers 1. HTML / JSX template — the visual structure: list container, card component, placeholder slots for each field. 2. CSS / styling — card appearance, status badge colours, spacing, responsiveness for mobile and desktop. 3. API call — GET /complaints?user={currentUser.id} to fetch complaint records from the server. 4. State management (React state, Redux, etc.) — store the fetched array, handle loading state, handle error state, trigger re-renders when data changes. 5. Data binding — map each complaint object's fields to the template slots: {complaint.complaint_desc}, {complaint.priority}. Total: 3–5 files, 150–300 lines of code, for one list screen. Any change to one layer often requires changes to the others.
documents.s: The Traditional Way of Building a UI

documents.t: ✅ The Page Builder replaces all five layers with a single metadata configuration In the Page Builder you configure the screen structure. The platform reads your configuration and generates the visual rendering, handles all data fetching, manages state automatically, applies your styling choices, and wires up the data bindings. This means: one tool, no files to keep in sync, no merge conflicts on screen structure, no state management code. The Page Wizard (used in this session) gives you a ready-made screen in minutes. Session 2 teaches you to build the same screen step-by-step so you understand every level of the hierarchy. Pages configured in the Page Builder render identically on both browser (web) and mobile (KloTouch) — no separate mobile codebase needed.

documents.t: A Business Object is a hierarchical tree of entities. The root entity represents the BO. Child entities are dependent on the root via Primary Relations. Before building screens, every developer must be familiar with the two core design tools in Klobase: the Data Studio (BOL Editor) and the Page Builder (UI Editor). documents.t: Navigate to Design Studio → Data Studio. The editor is divided into two major sections: the Tree on the left and the Detail on the right. documents.t: Navigate to Design Studio → Page Builder. According to the UI Editor 7.0 User Guide, the editor is divided into four major sections: Section What It Does Tree (Left) Hierarchical view of the entire page structure: Page → Page Layout → Page Area → Section → Controls. All creation, renaming, and assignment is done via right-click context menu in this tree. Preview (Centre) Live render of the screen. Refreshes on Save. Use the Auto Refresh toggle for real-time updates. Full Preview loads actual data from the database for testing. Detail (Down) Configuration panel for the selected tree element. Shows different properties depending on whether you have selected a Page, Page Layout, Page Area, Section, or Control. Page Data Model (Right — Tab) TransNode configuration. Defines what data is available to the page. Use the + button to add Model Paths. Each TransNode has: an ID, an Entity/Query binding, a Node Type (EntitySet / Entity / Query), and an optional Fold From parent. 📘 Page Builder Toolbar Reference (UI Editor 7.0 User Guide — Section 1.0) Edit icon — enables edit mode on the tree. You MUST click this before creating or renaming anything. + icon — create a new page (blank or from wizard). Save icon — commits all pending changes. Required before preview refreshes. Show Full Preview — loads real database records into the preview for testing. Detail icon — toggles visibility of the detail properties panel. Page Data Model icon — toggles visibility of the TransNode / data model panel. Reset Perspective — restores all panels to their default size and position. Preview In — switch preview between desktop, tablet, and mobile device views.
documents.s: B.2 — Page Builder (UI Editor) — Tool Layout

documents.t: Every screen in Klobase follows a strict 5-level hierarchy. This is the most important structural concept in UI development. Each level has a mandatory naming convention prefix: 📘 Five-Level Page Hierarchy Level 1 — PAGE (prefix: p_) The root container. Holds all layouts. Created first. One page can have multiple layouts (one per device type). At runtime, the platform picks the layout based on device: screencontainerdesktop, screencontainermobile, screencontainertab, screencontainerdefault. Level 2 — PAGE LAYOUT (prefix: pl_) Sits directly under the Page. Defines HOW the page areas are arranged. screenType options: stack, tab, two_column, object_page, grid_layout, hsplitter, vsplitter. Example: pl_complaints_desk (two column layout for desktop). Level 3 — PAGE AREA (prefix: pa_) A logical sub-container inside the layout. Can itself have a screenType (tab, stack, splitter). Sections are assigned to page areas to determine WHERE they render. Example: pa_complaints (list area), pa_complaint_details (detail area). Level 4 — SECTION (prefix: s_) The rendering unit. screenType determines HOW it displays data. Types: search, cardlist, card, form, grid, tree, timeline, map, calendar. Must be assigned to a Page Area to appear in the UI. Example: s_search (search), s_complaints (grid), s_detail_header (form). Level 5 — CONTROLS Individual fields, buttons, labels, icons bound to entity properties. Added via: right-click section → New → Controls, OR drag from unused TransNode properties. Section screenType Renders As search Filter bar with Close / Reset / Search buttons. Auto-generates the search toolbar. cardlist List of records as card rows — one card per record. Good for mobile and compact lists. grid Tabular list with column headers and rows. Supports sort, filter, group-by per column. form Detail form layout. Each control renders as a labelled input field. card Single entity rendered as a CSS grid card. One record only. tab Used on Page Areas to group child sections as tabs. showTitle must be true for tab labels. tree Hierarchical tree display for nested data.

documents.t: The Page Data Model defines the data available to a screen. Every section and control that displays data must be bound to a TransNode. A TransNode is a “data pipe” — it fetches entity records from the database and makes them available to sections and controls on the page. Node Type Fetches EntitySet A LIST of records. Use for search sections, grids, card lists. Suffix convention: _list. Example: d_complaints_list Entity ONE record (the currently selected record). Use for detail forms. Suffix convention: _detail. Example: d_complaints_detail Query Records from a kloQuery with WHERE conditions, joins, sorting. Suffix convention: _query. Other Non-standard / custom use cases. 📘 Fold From — The Critical Link Between List and Detail When you create d_complaints_detail (Entity type) and set its “Fold From” = d_complaints_list, the platform automatically loads the selected record’s data into d_complaints_detail whenever the user clicks a row in the list. This is the mechanism that connects list → detail. Without Fold From: the detail section will always be empty. With Fold From: clicking any complaint row in the list instantly populates the detail form. TransNode naming convention (from UI Editor 7.0 Guide): EntitySet → _list suffix Entity → _detail suffix Query → _query suffix

The Page Layout sits directly under the Page and defines the arrangement type for all page areas. According to UI Editor 7.0 Guide (Section 4.0): at runtime only one pageLayout is picked based on the device type — determined by the page’s screencontainerdefault, screencontainerdesktop, etc. properties. 1 In the tree, right-click on p_complaints → New → Page Layout. Press Enter. 3 Click pl_complaints_desk in the tree to open its Detail panel on the right. 4 In the Detail panel, set screenType = two column. This renders all assigned page areas one after another — the standard layout for list+detail screens. 5 Now click on p_complaints in the tree. In its Detail panel, set screencontainerdefault = pl_complaints_desk. This tells the platform: use this layout on all devices unless a device-specific layout is set. 6 Save. 📘 Layout Type Quick Reference (UI Editor 7.0 Guide — Section 12.0) stack — Sections / areas render one after another vertically. One subscreen shown at a time. two_column — Master-detail split: left panel (list) + right panel (detail). Max 2 columns. tab — Renders children as tabbed panels. Used at Page Area level for detail tabs. object_page — SAP-style object page: sticky header + tab body sections. hsplitter — Horizontal split with resizable rows. vsplitter — Vertical split with resizable columns. grid_layout / css_grid — CSS Grid-based placement. Requires modeller configuration.

An Entity Relation tells the Klobase server how two entities are connected to each other. Without a relation defined in the BOL Editor, the platform has no way to automatically load child records when a parent record is selected — and no way to bundle the BO for save/delete operations. There are two types of relations in Klobase: Relation Type What It Means Primary Relation Tight parent-child bond WITHIN the same Business Object (BO). A child entity is dependent on the parent. Prefixed pr_. Used for d_complaint_item, d_complaint_voices, d_complaints_attachment — all children of d_complaints. Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relation Looser link BETWEEN BOs. Used to reference standalone master entities. Prefixed r_. Used for d_customers and d_resp_team which are independent master entities. 📘 Why Relations Matter in the UI When a relation is defined and referenced in a TransNode in the Page Builder, the platform automatically fetches the child/linked entity records when the parent record is loaded. Without a relation, you would have to write manual queries and wire up the data fetch yourself. The TransNode type 'Relation' in the Page Data Model uses the relation name defined here — this is why naming the relation correctly matters. Naming convention (from BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Best Practices): pr_ prefix for primary relations, r_ prefix for associated/aggregated relations. Always lowercase.

documents.t: In Klobase, an Object Type (stored in the system property s_object_type) is a classification that tags each record as belonging to a specific type. Object Types serve two important purposes: They enable role-based visibility: a button or field can be made visible/editable only for a specific role AND a specific object type combination. This is used for screen behavior in Session 7. They allow ID Series to be object-type-specific: a different number series prefix can be applied per object type — for example, complaints created by Maventic employees might use a different prefix than those created by Procify employees. 📘 Object Type vs Object Group Object Group is a container that groups related Object Types together. The group is used as the filter boundary. Object Type is the actual tag applied to individual records (e.g. MAVENTIC, PROCIFY). Every Object Type must belong to exactly one Object Group. For the Customer Complaints application: Object Group = company_types Object Types = MAVENTIC, PROCIFY Best Practice (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide): Always maintain an Object Group to group types — the same group can be used in default filters based on users.

An ID Series is a platform-managed counter that automatically generates primary key values when a new record is created. Without an ID Series on complaint_id, a developer would need to generate unique IDs manually — which is error-prone and cannot produce readable, formatted numbers like CMP-00001. ID Series Type Description Auto Number Returns an incrementing number. Combined with a Prefix pattern to produce CMP-00001, CMP-00002, etc. GUID Returns a 32-character UUID. Good for distributed offline scenarios. Not human-readable. None No auto-generation. The developer or rule must set the key manually.

The complaint_id property now has an ID Series configured. 📘 ID Series Fields Reference (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Section 3.0.1 Creating ID Series) ID: Unique ID of the series. Naming convention: id_ prefix, all lowercase. Example: id_complaint. Type: Auto Number = incremental counter. Most common for business records. From: Starting number for the series. Use 1 to start from P-00001. Prefix: Text prepended before the number. P- produces P-1, P-2, etc. Chunk Size: Default 100. The server pre-allocates this many IDs per session (important for offline apps). Scope: Global (default) — one counter shared across all users and tenants. Pattern: Can be used to produce complex formats. For simple prefix + number, just use the Prefix field.

The system property s_status represents the current state of a complaint record. The Status tab in the Data Studio lets you define the allowed values for s_status and group them into Status Groups. Status Groups are named collections of statuses. They are used in Vienable (Session 7) to control screen behaviour: for example, the Edit button is visible only when s_status is in the OPEN_GROUP, and the Assign Team button is visible only when s_status is in the INPROCESS_GROUP. 📘 Status Lifecycle for Customer Complaints The complaint lifecycle defined in the BRD has 6 states: OPEN → INPROCESS → ON_HOLD / RESOLVED → CLOSED / REOPEN Each status transition is triggered by a specific role (defined in the Role Responsibility matrix from Session 1 Part A). In this session you define the status values and groups. The actual UI enforcement of transitions using Vienable happens in Session 7.

A Value Help (VH) is a platform-level component that provides a controlled list of choices for an entity property. When a VH is assigned to a property, the corresponding input field in the UI automatically renders as a dropdown (ComboBox), auto-complete field, or picker dialog (F4) — without any additional coding. The VH also validates that the entered value exists in the list when 'Is Restricted' is enabled. 📘 Three VH Types in Klobase (VH User Guide — Section 1.1) VH Config: Values are maintained in the metadata (config) DB. App-managed, flavor-dependent. Can be overridden by child apps. Requires a build after creation/update. Use for fixed classification lists (priority, complaint_type, etc.). VH Query: Values are fetched from a transactional or modelled query at runtime. Use for dynamic master data pickers (customer_id, responsible_team). The query determines what data appears in the picker. VH Transaction (DEPRECATED): Older type. Internally still supported for legacy apps. New development should use VH Config or VH Query instead. VH Type Source Naming Use Case for This App VH Config Metadata / Config DB vhc_<name> priority, complaint_type, nature_of_complaint VH Query Transactional / Modelled Query vhq_<name> customer_id → d_customers, responsible_team → d_resp_team

documents.t: A VH Query fetches its suggestion items from a live entity or modelled query at runtime. Unlike VH Config (which is static metadata), VH Query shows records that are currently in the transactional database. Key Property: The property whose value gets STORED in the parent entity when the user selects an item. For d_customers → customer_id. Display Text: The property shown to the user in the dropdown/picker. For d_customers → customer_name. Desc Format: How the display appears. Example: :customer_id--:customer_name shows ID followed by Name. Icon: Optional — entity property that holds an icon URL to show alongside each suggestion item.

documents.t: A KloQuery is the Klobase equivalent of a SQL SELECT statement. It lets you define — within the Data Studio — exactly what records to fetch, from which entity, with which filters, joins, and sort order. Unlike a Runtime Entity Query (which simply fetches all records of an entity), a Modelled Query gives you full control over the WHERE clause, JOIN entities, and sort order — and is reusable across multiple pages. Query Type When to Use Runtime Query (Entity Query) Fetch all records of a single entity. No WHERE clause in the definition. Filters applied at runtime via the TransNode. Use for simple list screens. Modelled Query (Dynamic Query) Define custom WHERE conditions, joins, sort order in the BOL Editor. Reusable, entity-independent. Use for role-filtered lists (My Complaints), VH Queries backed by joins, aggregated results. Native Query (Advanced Query) Raw SQL. Database-specific. Use only for special cases not achievable with modelled queries. Avoid training. 📘 KloQuery Fields Reference (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Section 3.0.2) Return Entity: The entity whose properties appear in the result set. Query Type: Runtime Entities And Join: Add the root entity and any joined entities (LEFT JOIN, INNER JOIN, etc.). Select Properties: Choose which properties from the entities appear in the result. Parameters: Define input parameters the query accepts at runtime (e.g., user_id filter passed from the TransNode). Where: Define filter conditions: entity.property = :parameter or entity.property = 'fixed_value'. Sort Order: Set the default sorting column and direction (ASC / DESC). Naming convention: Query IDs must start with q_. All lowercase.
Query ID Type Purpose q_complaints Modelled Employee: shows only complaints assigned to the logged-in user

A Saved Query is a named combination of a base query and a specific set of pre-filled search parameters. Where a Modelled Query defines the structure, a Saved Query defines a pre-configured instance of that query — ready to execute with one click in the search bar. Saved Queries appear as quick-filter options in the search TransNode of the UI. 📘 Saved Query vs Modelled Query (Basic Training Guide — Section 2.1) Modelled Query: The definition — entity, properties, parameters, WHERE logic. Reusable structure. Saved Query: A named configuration of a modelled query with preset parameter values. Stored per entity. In the UI, a Saved Query appears as a quick-filter button or dropdown in the search bar section. Saved Queries are created from the Data Browser (Advanced Search), not directly in the query detail tab. Naming convention for Saved Query IDs: Begin with sq_ by convention.

documents.t: The entity .ts file for d_complaints is located in the Private Node workspace at the path: workspace/apps/<your_app_id>/d_complaints.ts If the file does not exist yet, the private node can generate it. The base structure looks like this: import { KloEntity, ValidationError, ErrorType } from 'klobase'; export class d_complaints extends KloEntity { // ── Getters & Setters ────────────────────────────────────────── // ── Lifecycle Hooks ──────────────────────────────────────────── public async onAfterCreate(): Promise<any> { // Called after a new complaint record is created } public async OnValidate(): Promise<any> { // Called during navigation if transnode setActiveIf = Valid } public async onDelete(): Promise<any> { // Called after the record is deleted } } 💡 Architecture Principle: Business Logic Belongs Here The entity file is the authoritative location for all business logic. Period. Controller file → UI orchestration only (navigation, formatter functions, show/hide decisions). Entity file → field defaults, cross-field computations, validations, role enforcement. Never duplicate validation logic in the controller. If the controller calls commitP(), OnValidate() fires automatically on the server — that is your safety net. Reference: kloTouch 7.0 Basic Training Guide — Section 7.5 Best Practice Do's and Don'ts (Entity File).
documents.s: A.2 — Entity File Location and Structure

documents.t: Klobase provides three entity lifecycle hook methods that you override in the entity .ts file. These run on the server and are triggered automatically by the platform at the appropriate point in the entity's lifecycle. Method When Called Trigger Condition Primary Use onAfterCreate() After entity is created in DB On every new entity save Set defaults, auto-populate audit fields, initialise related records OnValidate() During navigation / on save / validateP function TransNode setActiveIf = 'Valid' Validate field values, enforce business rules, push errors onDelete() After entity is deleted On every delete operation Cascade cleanup, logging, send notifications 📘 OnValidate — Important Details OnValidate is triggered ONLY when the TransNode's 'setActiveIf' property is set to 'Valid' in the Page Builder. If setActiveIf is not set, OnValidate does NOT fire — the platform skips validation on navigation. Inside OnValidate, push errors using: this.errors.push(new ValidationError(this, propertyId, errorCode, message, ErrorType.ERROR)); The method must NOT return the errors array — it pushes to this.errors and the platform reads it. (PROC-24075 fixed this for proper return type.) ErrorType.ERROR blocks save. ErrorType.WARNING allows save but shows a warning toast. After your OnValidate runs, the platform ALSO runs its own mandatory-field validation based on key attributes — you don't need to repeat those.

Before OnValidate can fire, the TransNode that holds the complaint detail must be configured with setActiveIf = Valid in the Page Builder. # Action Detail / Code 1 Open Page Builder Navigate to Design Studio → Page Builder. Select customer_complaints_<prid>. Click the Edit icon. 2 Select the detail TransNode Click p_complaints in the tree. Open the Page Data Model panel. Click on the 'detail' TransNode row. 3 Set setActiveIf = Valid In the TransNode detail section (right side), find the 'setActiveIf' property. Change from the default (Always) to 'Valid'. This means: when the user tries to navigate away from the detail form, the platform will call OnValidate first. If errors exist, navigation is blocked. 4 Save Click Save.

documents.t: Rules contain business logic codes. It works with the event bus, any change in the entity will trigger the event, and all the rules hooked with the event will be executed sequentially. Rules are reusable objects across client, server and middleware. EX: When a complaint is created by an employee then status should be OPEN and assigned_to should be the same user. A responsible team/manager/assigned_to can be assigned by the manager only. An employee or manager can delete the complaint but not the responsible team Field Default Value Logic s_status 'OPEN' — every new complaint starts in OPEN status assigned_to this.txn.getUserID() — auto-set to the logged-in user who created the complaint created_on this.s_created_on — already auto-set by system field, no action needed created_by this.s_created_by — already auto-set by system field, no action needed

Step 1: Go to the Rule tab and click on the add icon(+). Field Description Event type Select the event type. Based on the type of event you choose, the rule will be executed. Type Select the channel type, based on this the transaction will be performed. Exit ID is an ID you put in for the rule subscription. (can select from the existing one). Clazz This will be the rule file name. Invocation Method The method needs to be called. Step 2: Select the Event Type from the drop-down. The event type will mention when the rules will be executed. Event types: On Create ( rule will be executed on create of an entity) On Delete (rule will be executed on delete of an entity) On Update (rule will be executed on update of an entity) Rest of the types will be covered in future. Step 3: Select the channel type(there are different input channels to perform a transaction on an entity, channel type selection decides when to trigger the Rule). Channel Type: Endpoint / Device on Klarion server- always on the client Endpoint / Device on Klarion server Endpoint / Device on Klarion server- always on server(current focus) Endpoint / Device to Server/ Client -Network Context Switch Legacy on Klarion server Klarion server to Klarion offline server Klarion server to Klarion Server Step 4: Fill in the value for Exit ID. Exit ID: It's an ID that you put in for the rule subscription. (can select from the existing one). Step 5: In the Clazz field provide the rule file name (example: rules/<file_name>) and in the invocation method provide an event name. You will be using that event to write your business logic codes. NOTE: If you are creating a Rule for the same entity you can fill this inside the Clazz field. Step 6: Click on the save button to save the newly created rule.

TypeScript property accessors let you intercept reads and writes of entity properties. In Klobase, setters and getters in the entity .ts file are the correct place for computed/derived field logic — not the controller. Pattern Purpose Setter (set propertyId) Called every time the property value changes. Use to: compute a derived field when an input changes, enforce value formatting, trigger side-effects. Getter (get propertyId) Called every time the property value is read. Use to: return a computed / formatted value instead of the raw stored value. ⚠ Critical Setter Pattern — Always Call this.s() Inside a setter, you MUST call this.s('propertyId', new_value, 'dataType', false, false) to actually persist the new value into the entity's internal state. Without this.s(), the new_value is accepted by TypeScript but never written to the entity data — the save will ignore your change. Pattern: if(new_value == this.propertyId) return; // guard to avoid infinite loop Then: this.s('propertyId', new_value, 'dataType', false, false);
documents.s: D.1 — What Are Setters and Getters?

documents.t: When a complaint is closed (closed_on is set), actual_tat should be computed as: (closed_on - created_on) in days. public set closed_on(new_value: Date) { if (new_value == this.closed_on) return; this.s('closed_on', new_value, 'date', false, false); // Compute actual_tat when closed_on is set if (new_value && this.s_created_on) { const msPerDay = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24; const diffMs = new Date(new_value).getTime() - new Date(this.s_created_on).getTime(); this.actual_tat = parseFloat((diffMs / msPerDay).toFixed(1)); } }
documents.s: D.2 — Setter: Auto-Compute actual_tat When closed_on Changes

documents.t: A getter can return a formatted composite string. For example, a display_title getter that combines complaint_id and priority: | // t_ prefix = transient property (not stored in DB) // Define t_display_title as a Transient property in the BOL Editor first public get t_display_title(): string { return `${this.complaint_id} [${this.priority || 'UNSET'}]`; } | | :---- | 📘 Transient Properties (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Entity Property Qualifier) Transient properties (t_ prefix) are computed at runtime and NOT stored in the database. They must still be defined as entity properties in the BOL Editor with qualifier = Transient. Once defined, they can be added to sections and controls in the Page Builder like any other property. The getter in the .ts file provides the value — the platform reads the getter whenever the control renders. Use transient properties for: display labels, formatted dates, computed totals, role-based display logic.

Part E — Query Rules E.1 — What are Query Rules? `Query rules are similar to Entity rules but are triggered before and after a query execution rather than around a create/update/delete. They are the correct place to answer two very different questions: Before the database is asked anything — “what should this user even be allowed to see?” (row-level filtering, defaulting search criteria). After the database has answered — “does the raw result need reshaping before it reaches the client?” (adding computed fields, merging data from a second query, masking sensitive values, sorting/aggregating in ways the query modeller can’t express. Both callbacks receive an EventContext (commonly named oEvent) and give access to the query instance itself via oEvent.getObject(). E.1 — How to Create Query Rules? Creating query rules is the same as creating entity rules, except the event type you subscribe to is one of: Event types: Before Query (beforeQ) — executes before the query is fired against the database. Anything set on the query object here becomes part of the WHERE condition. After Query (afterQ) — executes after results come back from the database, before they are returned to the client. The raw result set can be read and replaced here. Query Rule Event Reference (BOL API) Event.getObject() — returns the KloQueryForRule instance being executed. Set properties on it to add filter conditions (beforeQ), or call getResults() / setResults() on it to read/replace the raw result rows (afterQ). Event.getTxn() — returns the KloTransaction for the current user; use it to read $SYSTEM.roleID, call this.txn.get$User(), or check permissions. Event.getEventType() — returns which event fired, e.g. BEFORE_QUERY or AFTER_QUERY. Useful if one method is wired to handle both events. queryInstance.getResults() / setResults() — read or replace the raw JSON array of result rows in an afterQ callback. These are plain objects, not KloEntity instances — they cannot be saved back.

By the end of this session, you will be able to: Understand and apply all four binding modes in Klobase: Value, Path, Parts (with formatter), and Expression. Write expression bindings for visibility, enabled state, and dynamic text. Write and wire formatter functions in the controller. Every control on a Klobase screen reads and writes data through the Transaction Model ($M). The model is a JSON model object. All bindings use the prefix $M to reference it. Without a binding, a control shows a static value or nothing at all — it is disconnected from the live data.
documents.s: Part A — Data Bindings In Depth

documents.t: The Transaction Model is organized as a tree. Each TransNode in the Page Data Model corresponds to a branch in the $M tree. The full path to any property follows this pattern: {$M>/transNodeRelationId/propertyId} For a list TransNode with relationId = list, the first row's complaint_desc is: {$M>/list/0/complaint_desc} For the detail TransNode with relationId = detail: {$M>/detail/complaint_desc} The leading / after > is mandatory. Omitting it causes a silent bind failure.

Mode When to Use Syntax / Where to Set Example Value Static, hardcoded value — no model connection. Control always shows this literal text regardless of data. Properties tab → Value field text = 'Complaint ID' — always shows that label. Path Bind to exactly ONE model property. Two-way binding by default: changes in UI write back to model. Properties tab → DSRC field {$M>/detail/complaint_desc} — shows and edits the complaint description. Parts Combine MULTIPLE paths into one display value via a formatter function. Always one-way (read only). Properties tab → dsrc field (add each path as a part) + Formatter Function field Parts: {$M>/detail/first_name} + {$M>/detail/last_name} → formatter returns full name string. Expression Inline calculated value. No formatter function needed. Supports ternary operators and comparisons. Always one-way. Properties tab → dsrc field (starts with {= ...}) {= ${$M>/detail/is_escalated} === true ? 'Escalated' : 'Normal'} ⚠ Path and Parts are mutually exclusive on the same property — you cannot use both at once. If you need multiple values combined, always use Parts.

Path binding wires one control property to one model property. This is the most common binding type for form fields. # Action Detail 1 Select the control in the tree Example: select the complaint_desc m.Input control inside s_complaint_details section. 2 Open Properties tab Detail panel (right side) → Properties tab. 4 Enter the binding in dsrc Type: {$M>/detail/complaint_desc} — the detail TransNode relationId followed by the property ID. 5 Save and verify in Full Preview The field loads with the active complaint's description. Edit it and save — the new value persists in the database. 📘 The TransNode relationId is set in the Page Data Model, not the entity name. If your detail TransNode's relationId is complaints_detail, the path is {$M>/complaints_detail/complaint_desc}.

Use Parts when you need to combine or transform multiple model values into a single display string. Parts binding is one-way only — it cannot write back to the model. Value:​ The value field will hold the value provided for the property. Path:​ In this path field, users can only bind with exactly one property or value. This can be used if there is only one property to bind. Parts:​ In this path field, users can bind multiple properties or values. This can be used if multiple values or properties need to be provided for binding. (Note: If we are using formatter function, then it is mandatory to provide either parts or path value) Formatter Functions​ Controller function name (formatter function) can be given for the field. Type:​ In the type field, the user can provide the datatype for the control’s value. Formatter Options:​ Formatter options define how a value is formatted and displayed in the UI. Validation Constraint:​ Constraints are optional and define how an input value that is entered in the UI should look like. During parsing, the value is validated against these constraints. For example, an Integer type has a constraint for the maximum that is automatically validated when parsing the input values. Example: displaying TAT status as a composite string from actual_tat and standard_tat. // Controller function — formatTAT public formatTAT(actual: number, standard: number): string { if (!actual || !standard) return '—'; const diff = actual - standard; if (diff <= 0) return `✅ On Time (${actual} days)`; return `⚠ Overdue by ${diff} day(s) — Actual: ${actual}, SLA: ${standard}`; } ⚠ The formatter function receives Part values in the exact order they appear in the Parts list. If you add actual_tat first and standard_tat second, the function signature must be formatTAT(actual, standard).
documents.s: A.4 — Parts Binding with Formatter Function

documents.t: Expression binding lets you write a JavaScript ternary expression directly inside a binding path string. It starts with {= and ends with }. It is evaluated live at runtime whenever the bound model values change.

Rule Detail Starts with {= The expression must begin with {= (curly brace, equals). Without the =, it is treated as a plain path, not an expression. Reference model paths with ${} Inside an expression, wrap every $M path in ${}: ${$M>/detail/s_status}. This dereferences the path to its current value. Must return a value The expression must evaluate to a value matching the property type. visible expects boolean. text expects string. enabled expects boolean. Ternary only for simple cases Use condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Complex multi-branch logic belongs in a formatter function, not in expression binding. No function calls You cannot call controller functions from expression binding. Use Parts + formatter for that.

Use Case Property Expression Explanation Show Save/Cancel only in EDIT or CREATE mode visible {= ${$M>/TransactionMode } === 'EDIT' Make Edit button invisible in EDIT mode visible {= ${$M>/TransactionMode } === 'DISPLAY' ? true : false} Edit button should disappear the moment the user clicks it and mode switches to EDIT. Show escalation badge only when escalated visible {= ${$M>/detail/is_escalated} === true ? true : false} is_escalated is a Boolean property. Bind to the is_escalated path directly. Dynamic text: 'Escalated' vs empty text {= ${$M>/detail/is_escalated} === true ? 'ESCALATED' : ''} Shows ESCALATED label text conditionally. Returns empty string otherwise. Disable complaint_desc when not OPEN enabled {= ${$M>/detail/s_status} === 'OPEN' ? true : false} The complaint description should only be editable when the complaint is in OPEN status. Dynamic placeholder label for priority text {= ${$M>/detail/priority} === 'VERY_HIGH' ? '🚨 Critical' : ${$M>/detail/priority}} Shows emoji label for critical priority, falls back to raw value for others. TAT warning color class {= ${$M>/detail/actual_tat} > ${$M>/detail/standard_tat} ? 'tat-overdue' : 'tat-ok'} Applies different CSS class depending on whether actual exceeds standard TAT. ⚠ Expression binding is evaluated once per model change event. For heavy computation (e.g. comparing arrays or doing date math), use a formatter function instead — expression binding performance degrades with complex logic.
documents.s: B.2 — Expression Binding Examples (Customer Complaints App)

documents.t: A formatter function is a TypeScript method in the controller file that takes one or more raw model values as input and returns a formatted display value. It is the right tool whenever expression binding would become too long, needs multi-step logic, or needs to look up external data.

Formatter functions are public methods on the controller class. They must be public — the framework calls them reflectively from the Page Builder binding. export class p_complaints extends KloController { // Formatter functions — called from Parts binding in Page Builder public formatPriority(priority: string): string { const map: Record\<string,string\> \= { 'LOW': '🟢 Low', 'MEDIUM': '🟡 Medium', 'HIGH': '🔴 High', 'VERY\_HIGH': '🚨 Very High' }; return map\[priority\] || priority || '—'; } }

Function Name Input Parts Return Example Output formatPriority(priority) {$M>/detail/priority} string 🔴 High formatTAT(actual, standard) {$M>/detail/actual_tat}, {$M>/detail/standard_tat} string ⚠ Overdue by 3 day(s) formatStatusLabel(status) {$M>/detail/s_status} string 🟠 IN PROCESS formatFullName(first, last) {$M>/detail/created_by_first}, {$M>/detail/created_by_last} string John Doe formatEscalationText(isEsc, type) {$M>/detail/is_escalated}, {$M>/detail/complaint_type} string ESCALATED — BILLING formatDateAge(createdOn) {$M>/detail/created_on} string 3 days ago

documents.t: # Action Detail 1 Write the function in controller.ts Open the controller file in Online Code Editor. Add a public method with the formatter logic. Ensure it takes the exact number of parameters as the number of Parts you will add. 2 Select the target control Page Builder → select the control whose display property you want to format (e.g. m.Text for priority display). 3 Delete existing Path binding If a Path binding exists on the property, clear it first — Parts and Path cannot coexist. 4 Switch to Parts Properties tab → click Parts radio button. 5 Add each Part in order Click + for each model path. Order matters: Part 1 = first function argument, Part 2 = second argument, etc. 6 Set Formatter Function field Type the exact function name as it appears in the controller. No parentheses, no 'this.' prefix. 7 Private Node must be running Formatter function calls go to the running Private Node. Start your Private Node before testing. Without it, the binding silently returns undefined. 8 Save and Full Preview The control should now render formatted output. Open Chrome DevTools Sources to debug if the output is wrong. ⚠ Formatter functions must be PURE — they should not modify model state, call APIs, or have side effects. They are called repeatedly on every model refresh. Side effects cause unpredictable behavior and performance issues.
